The house resumed from Tuesday, February 7, consideration in committee of Bill No. 19, to amend the Migratory Birds Convention Act -Mr. Murphy-Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 2-Royal Canadian Mounted Police to be game officers.

When the committee adjourned I understand the specific question under consideration was that asked by my hon. friend the member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) whether the Minister of Justice would consider specifying individual members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to be migratory bird officers, instead of a blanket authority conferred upon the whole force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I remember the discussion that took place. I think the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth urged two points; one in regard to clothing members of the police with magisterial powers. I am inclined to agree with the objection which he took in that respect. I do not think that members of the police who are designated as officers under the Migratory Birds Convention Act should be clothed with the powers of magistrates. And as I read the act now carefully I do not think the act gives them such powers, though 53719-131
that power was conferred upon those who were appointed under the present act.
On the other point that the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth urged, that certain members of the mounted police force should be designated in each province as inspectors under the Migratory Birds Convention Act, I have discussed this with the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and he is utterly opposed to the suggestion. He says that if such a proposal were adopted the tendency would be for members of the force to imagine that was their particular work, and they would disregard other services which they were called upon to perform. He says it is one of the cardinal rules of the force that its members shall enforce in general all the laws of the country or the province, and shall not be designated for any specific branch of the service. We have the preventive service, for instance; in certain provinces they do work under the liquor laws. He is utterly opposed to segregating any part of the service for any special law enforcement, and he objects for that reason to the proposal made by my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth. He says it will be far more satisfactory to allow the whole force to become inspectors under the Migratory Birds Convention Act, so that it will become the duty of every member to enforce that as well as other laws.

When
this act is passed, will the enforcement of the provisions rest with the Department of Justice or with the Department of the Interior as heretofore?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If it rests with any department I would fancy it would rest with the Department of Justice, because the Migratory Birds Convention Act enforcement has now been transferred by order in council to the Department of Justice, being the department, in control of the mounted police. I assume that all prosecutions would be under that department in the future.

May I ask
then if all the officers will be transferred from the Department of the Interior to the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That has already been
done.

The Migratory Birds
Convention Act, interpretation clause states that the minister for the purpose means the Minister of the Interior; that has not been changed. The order in council .simply transfers to the Department of Justice the police work, carrying out the regulations, dealing with illegal shooting.

2074	COMMONS
Migratory Birds Convention Act
In order to clear the matter up I will read the clause of the order in council, being P.C. 2283-

When
was that passed?

Friday, October 14, 1932.
The clause reads:
Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Justice and under the provisions of section 2	(a) of chapter 165, revised statutes of
Canada, 1927, is pleased to order that the responsibility for the police work in connection with the enforcement of the provisions of the Migratory Birds Convention Act and regulations thereunder throughout Canada be and it is hereby transferred from the Department of the Interior to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. All other responsibilities under the said act to remain with the Department of the Interior.
According to the terms of the order in council the Department of Justice, through the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, will be charged with the police duties, but other phases of the act will continue to be enforced by the minister of the Department of the Interior.

AVhat
will the other responsibilities be that will remain with the Department of the Interior when the actual enforcement of the provisions of the act is transferred to the Department of Justice?

The Migratory Birds
Convention Act was passed following an agreement between this country and the United States for the conservation of the wild bird life of this continent, dealing solely with migratory birds. There are many other duties beyond that of merely police work in protecting the birds from illegal shooting during certain ^seasons of the year. It is a much broader question, it deals with the conservation of the wild bird life of this continent, which is very important. One phase of the duties would be the establishment, as has been done, of sanctuaries throughout Canada where no shooting is allowed. Also studies of the habits of these birds, in order that a proper understanding may be had of them with a view to necessary regulation or legislation for their conservation and increase. Merely protecting them from illegal shooting is only a small part, I would say, of the duties of the Department of the Interior in conserving these birds.

That does not do away with the argument I advanced the other day about conflict of jurisdiction. I do not want
 .
to go over the ground again, but I believe I [DOT]showed the other day that in the application of that law there will be conflict between federal and provincial jurisdictions. I believe that could be cured by an amendment, after the words "game officers"-
in districts and territories where the federal government has full jurisdiction.
I know from personal knowledge of many occasions in northern Ontario when conflict has arisen-not open rivalry, because I say here that all mounted police are glad to work in cooperation with municipal and provincial police. But I believe there is an anomaly there which should be remedied. Surely the federal government does not want to interpose its authority where a province has full jurisdiction. I believe that amendment would do away with a lot of criticism and things that have happened in the past.
The Minister of Justice in answer to my question said it was within the authority of the federal government, in the case of an international treaty of this nature, to impose upon the provinces the application of that law. So why the conflict of authority? I do not see the necessity of it, and I take it the Minister of Justice and also the Minister of the Interior want to avoid any friction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my hon. friend's anticipation of friction is purely imaginary. His amendment would confine the federal jurisdiction to rvha,t we know as the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. The rest of this country is allotted to the various provinces who have sovereign rights in their respective portions. There is no conflict of jurisdiction with regard to an international treaty, the federal government being vested with power to carry out in the various provinces the provisions of such treaties. I cannot imagine that there will be any conflict between the provincial and federal authorities with regard to this particular convention. If my hon. friend's amendment were to carry the jurisdiction of the federal authorities would be confined to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Protection is not nearly so necessary in those parts of Canada as it is in the more settled portions where there are more sportsmen and more guns. It is to protect the migratory birds in these districts that this convention is framed.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two observations with regard to this bill. In the first place I am opposed to a division of jurisdiction between the Department of the Interior and the Department of Justice

Migratory Birds Convention Act
in connection with the enforcement of the provisions of this bill and the conservation of wild game. I am opposed also, by inference, to the suggestion which, according to the Minister of Justice, has been made by the commissioner of the mounted police to the effect that it would be a bad principle to appoint specific men by name. I have the greatest respect for this officer but I contend that parliament should decide these questions and not any gentleman who happens to be the head of the mounted police. I do not say it is deliberate, but there does seem to be a tendency to take away from various departments of government certain powers which are turned over to the mounted police. It is possible to go too far in this direction. The provisions of the old bill were better in every way. Under the present bill I think there will be a conflict in authority. It is all very well to say that it is only the policing that is being vested in the Deportment of Justice, but the fact remains that there were very few complaints against the old game officers under the Department of the Interior. I am afraid too much authority is being vested in the mounted police. Lost year they took over the preventive service, it is now being proposed that they shall take over the migratory bird service and next year it may be something else. I wish to sound a word of warning against the vesting of too much authority in the mounted police of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, supplementing what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has so well said as to there being no conflict of jurisdiction in these matters, I wish to say that the provinces and the dominion have always worked in the fullest cooperation. There has been no conflict in enforcing the provisions of the act or establishing closed seasons during certain periods of the year. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) fears that the jurisdiction is being divided, but may I say that we are only doing now in the maritime provinces what has been done in all parts of Canada during the past years. Last year the mounted police took over the duties previously performed by the provincial police in the provinces of the west. The enforcement of the police regulations of this act, if I may so term them, was carried out by the provincial officers in the western provinces and last year this work was taken over by the mounted police. We are only doing now in the maritime provinces what has been done throughout the rest of the country.
53719-131J

Is that
done specifically or generally?

It has been general in each province. In the province of Ontario the provincial police officers have been in the main enforcing the police regulations of this act, as was the case in the western provinces until last year, when the provincial police duties were taken over by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I do not think there is any basis for the fears of my hon. friend.

Mr. Chairman, with
what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) I agree fully in so far as the taking away of further rights from the provinces is concerned. As one who delights in spending as much time as he can during the proper seasons in the bush and on the streams, I think it is a great mistake to change the officials who have been administering this law. In the districts with which I am acquainted, I think the law has been administered very efficiently. It has been my good fortune to have travelled extensively in the Gatineau valley and north of Maniwaki, and I have always found that the officials in Quebec were looking after their duties in a most efficient manner. I have the greatest admiration for that very wonderful corps called the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and I know how efficiently they discharge all duties entrusted to them. I have no doubt that they would be able to carry out such duties as are required under this act in an efficient manner as far as the urban and more thickly settled districts are concerned, but I do not think this would apply to the more thinly populated sections. These game wardens travel by canoe and on foot over every inch of their country, they have the qualifications and the aptitude to discharge their duties, and I do hope that these men will be maintained in their present positions. I do not think the mounted police would be able to perform these duties as efficiently as the present game wardens.

With all due respect to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) I must tell him and the house that I know from personal experience that there have been many instances of conflict between the two authorities in northern Ontario. I should like to quote from Hansard at page 1777. I asked the minister the following question:
I would ask the Minister of Justice: This act we ate dealing with being an international matter, is there in the constitution machinery which will allow the federal government to ask the provincial governments to apply this act?
2076	COMMONS
Migratory Birds Convention Act
The Minister of Justice replied:
There is a provision in our constitution that in regard to international treaties the federal government can enact laws imposing upon a province whatever is necessary to carry out an international obligation. This being an international obligation, a matter of treaty between Canada and the United States, the federal government is empowered to pass such laws as are necessary to put it into force in the various provinces of Canada.
When you have two police bodies, the provincial police and the mounted police, there is bound to be conflict if they are both given the same jurisdiction. I should like to inquire of the minister if the officers of the mounted police would be also justices of the peace?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
If they are to have no jurisdiction in the imposing of fines, then the conflict would not be so great.

For the reasons mentioned when this bill came up before, I think it is my duty to protest once more against the enactment of this legislation. As I pointed out at that time, I think this power, if put into force, will have the effect of depriving of their livelihood many humble people in my constituency who earn their living by having been appointed under the authority of the Department of the Interior to enforce the law under the direction of Mr. Lewis. It is not fair of the government to take such action. I see in it also a certain kind of propaganda the government wants to spread, because when these officials of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are appointed to patrol a whole district, they will have in a way a say at election times. Although I do not know whether all those who have been appointed of recent years to the mounted police are of any one political party, there is no doubt that when they will have charge of the enforcement of the law in those districts, they will be much more severe on the people there than would the officials who were formerly appointed. Those who were appointed before under the direction of Mr. Lewis were men who knew the territory in which they were serving, and so far I have not heard of any complaint against them or against the work which Mr. Lewis has been performing in that district.
As I said before, the government in these matters every year brings in too much legislation giving most extensive powers and territory to cover to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I quite agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre when he said that year after year new legislation is introduced giving broader powers to

the mounted police. I may put it in a word, as I said the other day, that the government seems to have gone mad on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I do not think the government will gain anything by amending the law in the way they want to do.

In looking
over Bill No. 19, to amend the Migratory Birds Convention Act, it would seem to transfer to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police the enforcement of the recommendations contained in the Migratory Birds convention. I understand that laws are passed in this house and then most of them are left to the provinces to enforce. In our province of Quebec we have special legislation covering the protection of migratory birds and game; we have also our own game keepers appointed under provincial laws, to enforce our legislation. According to the proposed measure, members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are to be made game wardens. The result will be, for instance, if a mounted police officer, appointed under this legislation as a game warden, sees at a railway station or a wharf, some game, he will bring the offender before a police court magistrate. Then the court will be open to receive a writ of certiorari, and a writ of summons and a petition declaring a statement of claim that the legislation that is being passed this afternoon should be declared ultra vires.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This bill does not propose to interfere in any way with the local game laws of any province or with the enforcement of those laws. The only proposal in this bill is to change the nature of the inspectors from civilians who have been appointed heretofore to members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

I gathered
from the minister's remarks that those police officers were not to be magistrates, but I see section 2 reads:
Subsection one of section 5 of the said act is amended by adding at the end thereof the following words:
"All members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police shall, for the purpose of this act, be ex officio game officers."
I see that section 5, subsection one, at present reads as follows:
The minister may appoint game officers for carrying out this act and the regulations, and may authorize such game officers to exercise the powers of a justice of the peace or the powers of a police constable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Those are the ones appointed in that way. I made the same mistake

Migratory Birds Convention Act
as my hon. friend has made. Those were game wardens appointed under the act as it stood:
The minister may appoint game officers for carrying out this act and the regulations, and may authorize such game officers to exercise the powers of a justice of the peace or the powers of a police constable.
The mounted police are not appointed by the minister. They are appointed, according to the amendment, as follows:
All members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police shall, for the purpose of this act, be ex officio game officers.
Consequently they will not be justices of the peace.

I should like to ask the
Minister of the Interior what the relations will be between the chief migratory game officer and the members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In the maritime provinces, for example, there is a chief migratory game officer, Mr. Robie Tufts, of Wolfville, Nova Scotia, and in that province there are some 150 members of the mounted police who are under the control of the Department of Justice. Will Mr. Tufts have authority to select any one or more of the members of the mounted police and direct them to go into particular locations, watch for offenders and lay charges? In other words, are they to be under his direction? If so, have you not officials who are controlled by the Department of Justice under the authority of superior officers who are controlled by the Department of the Interior? Perhaps the minister could explain that.

I do not anticipate any
difficulty on that score because we have in the western provinces an official of the department in the person of Mr. Munro who exercises the same powers as does Mr. Tufts in Nova Scotia. We have also in the person of Mr. Lewis at Ottawa a permanent migratory bird warden who exercises for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec the same powers as do these other two men. These men simply cooperate with the police force, whatever it may be, in enforcing the regulations in regard to illegal shooting. There should therefore be no difficulty in the matter. The chief officer of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and Mr. Tufts will no doubt work in close cooperation, and * Mr. Tufts from his long experience will be able to advise that officer as to the steps which should be taken to protect those birds. But as regards the mounted police taking orders, certainly they will take their orders as such from their superior officer in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
It seems to me that is going to interfere with the administration of the act.
It does not.

It is very' important that
the chief migratory game officer should have a deciding voice as to what information should be laid and what prosecution should be undertaken. By this legislation his powers are taken away from him. If this is to be the effect; if he has cooperating with him and not working under him officers who are charged with the duty of apprehending offenders and laying informations and yet he has not any power over those officers, then you are going to have a division of responsibility which does not make for good enforcement of the act. I do not know anything about conditions in the other provinces, but this is very important in the maritimes and perhaps more important in Prince Edward Island than in Nova Scotia. I am not sure whether Prince Edward Island is policed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it is.

Well, the same condition
will arise there. I am of opinion that the enforcement of the act will not be as effective with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police not subject to the authority of the chief migratory game officer for the district as it is under the present system. In my own province the chief migratory bird officer is an enthusiast and he commands the respect of everybody who knows anything about the enforcement of the act. He knows from experience the sort of men who will work efficiently under him, and he has built up an efficient staff which now is going to be taken away from him entirely, and instead he is to be supplied with certain officers of another department over which he has no actual authority, and he is going to be charged with the administration of the act in his district. It seems to me that this change will not make for efficiency.

I ^should like to make a brief observation to the house, and that is that if there were a few more game conservationists throughout Canada of the kind found in my riding you could dispense with all your Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers and all your game wardens. It is in the county which I have the honour to represent that Jack Miner has established his bird sanctuary, and I challenge all the representatives in this house to show that all your game vardens

Migratory Birds Convention Act
and all your mounted police officers can protect more birds than Jack Miner does in his sanctuary.

Has the
Minister of Justice received any objection from the attorney general of the province of Quebec to the passing of this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, none whatever.

It is very convenient
sometimes not to have a legal mind. Personally I am not very much concerned over the legal aspects of this bill. I think myself that the bill is a decided step forward, and the only thing the matter with it so far as I can see is that it does not include nonmigratory birds as well as migratory.
They are under provincial law.

So much the better. I
come from a province which boasts one of the finest game birds in the world, the prairie grouse.
The prairie grouch?

I do not believe there
is any better game bird in Canada than our prairie chicken in the fall, but I regret to say that we have had on two or three occasions to close the season for grouse hunting for a period of several years because the birds have become so depleted. I honestly believe that the depletion was not caused by legal hunting, but because certain citizens of Manitoba insisted on shooting the birds in season and out of season all the year round. To a very large extent the rural citizens in certain districts of Manitoba-and I do not blame them so much because they feed the birds- shoot the prairie chicken twelve months in he year. As is well known, the mounted police have the habit of going out and getting their man which the old game wardens did not have, and I think it is a mighty fine thing to have the mounted police on the trail of the offender under this act.

Section agreed to.
On the preamble.

Has section four been
passed, Mr. Chairman?

Hon. T. G. MURPHY (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 21, to amend the Indian Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 1.-Truant officers.
Would the minister explain this section?

As the hon. member
doubtless knows, we have both residential and day schools established on the reserves throughout Canada for the purpose of educating 'Indian children. The services of a truancy officer are not required to any great extent, if at all, for the residential schools, but in the case of the day schools the services of a truancy officer are sometimes required. On some of the reserves we have special constables who perform this duty among their other duties, but on other reserves there are no such special officers, and it has been the custom in the past to appoint members of the mounted police for this duty. This section simply blankets in the force to carry out this duty wherever their services may be required.
Would the minister explain what the powers of a truancy officer are as defined in the section?

Subsection 3 of section 10 of the act reads:
The Superintendent General may appoint any officer or person to be a truant officer to enforce the attendance of Indian children at school, and for such purpose a truant officer shall be vested with the power's of a peace officer, and shall have authority to enter any place where he has reason to believe there are Indian children between the ages of seven and fifteen years, and when requested by the Indian agent, a school teacher or the chief of a band shall examine into any case of truancy, shall warn the truants, their parents or guardians or the person with whom any Indian child resides, of the conse-

Indian Act
quences of truancy, and notify the parent, guardian or such person in writing to cause the child to attend school.
Evidently this seotion is directed towards day school attendance?
Yes.

Has the
minister considered the objection there might be towards having a uniformed mounted police offioer going to an Indian home to asoertain whether or not the children have been detained by action of the parents? I am inclined to believe that the proposed section is drastic?

In years past mounted police officers have performed those duties in various places. As I said a moment ago, on certain reserves we have special constables, but on others we have not those constables, and in such cases need the services of some offioer. I must say the phase of the matter to which the hon. member has referred did occur to me in connection with the proposed amendment. My view however was that for years past mounted police officers have been performing very wide duties, and enforcing many laws throughout Canada. I cannot conceive that the sight of a mounted police uniform, one which must be familiar to the eyes of all Canadians including Indians, would raise any undue alarm in the breasts of those people.
Is it the intention of the government to formulate a similar provision with regard to the Douk-hobor children who refuse to attend school?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a hard nut to crack.
The enforcement of attendance of white children rests with the provincial authorities.

I know of reserves in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec where they have their own school boards. I believe that condition applies at Caughnawaga, and at some points in Ontario. It may be that the proposed change will conflict with local laws, because if I understand school legislation properly, and more particularly in connection with the province of Ontario, the school board has power to appoint truant officers, and the same legislation would apply to reserves. I do not suppose it applies at points such as Caughnawaga where there are only Indians, and where there may be no
school boards. In the older reserves, however, it is my information that there are school boards, and that those bodies have the power to appoint truant officers. What provision is to be made in such cases?
If the children are attending school there will be no difficulty.

Is it proper to teach
children to have no respect for authority?

I am quite well aware that this matter has given the department some considerable worry. The fact that on the one hand school teachers are paid, schools established, and on the other that parents connive to prevent the attendance of their children at school, must present real difficulty. The only question which arises in my mind is one concerning the advisability of uniformed officers performing the duties of truant officers. I can well imagine that in some instances where they perform special duties, they might do so without difficulty. I am doubtful however as to the advisability of this measure, and while it may be necessary to send mounted police officers to reserves to enforce laws, the matter now under discussion is of a somewhat different nature. I do not know what the experience of the minister has been, but my experience in the administration of the act was that the fault was usually that of the parents, and never that of the child. The parents keep their children away from school, a difficulty which does not arise in connection with boarding schools, but arises in connection with day school attendance. I believe it is inadvisable to use Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers for the performance of these rather petty duties.

I believe when the hon. member was in charge of the department police officers visited the reserves. The police are changed from time to time, as they are moved around. To get rid of the difficulty of swearing in a new man as a truant officer it was proposed to insert a general clause in the act allowing any officer to act as a truant officer. It has been represented that the proposed change would have the effect of saving some money, and would make general a practice which has been developing throughout the last ten or fifteen years.
Mr. LaVERGNE: I have high respect for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a body of men of which we ought to be proud. I feel however that if the present legislation were passed we would be encroaching upon provincial rights, and would be going beyond the provisions of section 93 of the British North America Act, which provides:
In and for each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education.
And so on. That is the principle of the section. The people in any province are subject to the provincial laws concerning education. I may be wrong, but I am taking this opportunity of placing my views before the committee. If I am wrong, so much the better. In the province of Quebec there is a Huron reserve, in connection with which there is a school commissioner and a school board. Rightly or wrongly-and I think rightly-in that province we are opposed to compulsory education. A truant officer or a Royal Canadian Mounted Police constable could, under the proposed legislation, enter one of our reserves and enforce compulsory education, contrary to the laws of our province. For that reason I believe we are on dangerous ground. There is but one matter in connection with education left to federal power, and that pertains to the rights of minorities. It would seem that that section of the British North America Act has been forgotten on many occasions. It is my view that making a Royal Canadian Mounted Police constable a truant officer, and conferring upon him special power concerning Indians, is encroaching upon a matter which should be left entirely in the hands of provincial authorities. The British North America Act is an imperial statute and is supreme; in this committee we are bound to respect every clause of it. In a matter of school rights, which, by our constitution, are 
left entirely within the control of the provinces, we should be very careful before interfering or extending further authority to Royal Canadian Mounted Police or other truant officers. The bill before us relates only to Indians, but in the light of section 93 of the British North America Act I doubt very much, if we have any authority to create truant officers to act in any province against the laws of that province. I ask the committee to be very careful before making a definite decision.

I should like to support
every word that has been said by my hon. friend from Montmagny. This is not only a matter of school rights; it is also a matter of the rights of parents, and as a French-Canadian I am rather afraid. If my hon. friend from Long Lake (Mr. Cowan) were Minister of the Interior, for instance, would he consider the French-Canadians as Indians? Would we be looked after by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police? I have been arguing for liberty. I have great respect for my good friend the Minister of the Interior and also for my friend the Minister of Justice; I should be very sorry to be unpleasant to them, but the rights of the provinces must be respected, and the rights of individuals must be respected as well. I wonder if we are taking the right course now. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are looking after migratory bird*s; now they are to look after the Indians. What will be next?
I would suggest that legislation of this kind is nonsensical at this stage of the session. We are here to deal with the problems which concern the nation, but this question does not interest the nation. We are waiting our time discussing it, but we have to discuss it in order to defend the rights and privileges of our Canadian citizens. The Indians were the first inhabitants of this country. They do not have the right to vote, but they are fellow citizens. I think it is a very bad thing to open the door through which our liberties may disappear. To-day it i*s the Indians; what will come next? That is the whole question.

I am glad to say that the Riviere du Loup station has been fixed, and well fixed. I should like to ask a
question about ownership by individual Indians. It has always been my impression that animals, implements and so on placed with the band by the government belong to the band as a band and do not become the property of any individual Indian.

I am speaking without the advice oi my official, but in regard to ownership of cattle w-hich have been purchased from time to time either by the government from parliamentary appropriations or from band funds, I am not certain in the first instance as to where the ownership rightfully belongs. But I can tell my hon. friend this, that when cattle, placed in charge of the individual Indian, are sold the proceeds go to the individual Indian.

I notice that section 3 of
the bill provides for an amendment to the act concerning sale of cattle, whereas section 4 relates to the sale of grains, roots and crops; then section 9 provides for a penalty. As the . minister explained it, this affects only the western provinces. May I call to the attention of the minister the reverse aspect of that. I am ready to admit that this amendment is an improvement in this respect, that the Indian will be liable to punishment if he sells his cattle oT crops without the permit of the agent, but there is no provision of the Indian Act for any penalty or responsibility when the Indian buys from white people. For instance, an Indian may buy an automobile or whatever he likes, and as the hon. minister said a few minutes ago he is quite conversant with his irresponsibility, he laughs at his creditors. It goes further than that. I have a reverse in my riding, at Caughnawaga. As a matter of fact the majority of the Indians are good citizens, honest, industrious and very skilful in certain kinds of work; but, as in any other community, a certain number being familiar with and taking advantage of their impunity under the law do injury to the whole community. I suggest that where Indians take advantage of their irresponsibility the law should require them to pay for whatever they buy or whatever damage they cause. I have in mind an instance of an Indian farm with, of course, no fences or ditches around it, situated in the neighbourhood of the property of a citizen of the parish of St. Constant. If cattle happen to pass from one farm to another an animal may be

seized by the Indian and sold for his own use. If the owner of the animal takes action against the Indian and tries to execute his judgment he is just laughed at; the Indian is not responsible! If we apply to the department the department answers,-very rightly, because the law is so construed:-We have nothing to do with that. So the irresponsibility of the Indian under the law is abused by those on the reserve who do not respect the law at all. .
In summing up my remarks I would like to know from the hon. minister if it would not be advisable to insert in the act a section covering such cases.

As to the responsibility
of Indians generally for debts contracted in the ordinary course of business, I would imagine that all merchants and others having dealings with Indians are fully aware that in selling to an Indian on credit they are taking long chances. In other words, the Indian is considered as a minor, a ward, and the only method I can conceive of whereby that particular Indian could be made responsible for his debts would be to enfranchise him and make him a citizen, in which case he would be amenable to the laws and subject to be sued in court.
As to the other point, the straying of animals on reserves, there is provision in the Indian Act whereby such animals should be impounded, as they are in any other locality, and after due advertisement sold. I cannot conceive of an Indian, merely because an animal has strayed on the reserve, selling that animal and using the proceeds, without being subject to procedure in the courts.
That is the fact.

I cannot argue the legal
aspect, I am not a lawyer, but I think that would be only common sense and I believe good law.

In answer to the argument of the hon. minister, when he compares the Indian to a minor, if the law so regards him the comparison should be continued. An individual who is a minor has a guardian and if the minor does something wrong the father or guardian is responsible for his act. But in the case of the Indian the Department of Indian Affairs takes no responsibility for the mischief the Indian does. So I believe there is something wrong. Then the hon. minister says that people in general must know that when they deal with an Indian they deal at their own risk. As the minister knows, these Indians do not always stay upon the reserves. They come to Montreal or to Laprairie and

Indian Act
it is hard to tell them from white men. Many of them own automobiles, they obtain licences and go driving through the country and when an accident occurs they attempt to escape liability by saying to the injured party, "I am not responsible, I am a minor."
Mr. BURY': So does a minor.

That is the answer given to many who suffer injuries in collisions with the cars of these Indians. The extent of the damages may amount to two or three thousand dollars, it may be that even a death occurs, but they attempt to escape liability in this manner. I must say that many of these Indians will try to cover any damages which might occur, but there are some of them who try to escape. I do not think that the Indians or the Department of Indian Affairs should be above the law in such matters.

I endorse what the hon. member has just said. I do not see why a colour line should be drawn; I see no reason why certain Indians should not be given the franchise. Many of them are very intelligent, many conduct different kinds of businessea Those who fought in the war were enfranchised but in many cases they have brothers and sisters who are just as intelligent and as ambitious as they are. I suggest to the minister that he consider seriously the enfranchising of those Indians who are capable of exercising their rights. There are two bands in my riding made up of intelligent and industrious people. They follow different lines of occupation and yet they are treated as minors or wards of the government. I remember very distinctly one bright boy coming to me and telling me how he was handicapped because he was an Indian. He was very ambitious and had saved enough money to buy a motor car, but he found he could get no work to do. When he applied for work he was told that as the work available was for relief purposes and as he was a ward of the government he could not be given anything to do. He was very ambitious and ready and willing to work, yet he could obtain nothing. Providing an Indian has the necessary intelligence, I think he should be given the rights of citizenship. I suggest that many white men are not capable of exercising their rights, and I think an effort should be made to see if we cannot make a better citizen out of the Indian.
There is another matter I should like to take up with the minister, although it may not be exactly germane to the present discussion. I think the department should exercise greater care over the health of the Indian. I am told that throughout the northern parts of Ontario
tuberculosis is sweeping the Indians into eternity by the hundreds. A doctor visits these Indians once a year, he leaves certain medical supplies but in the meantime they have to doctor themselves just as they have to feed themselves. As long as they remain wards of the government, the government has a responsibility which should be exercised in as humane a way as possible.
I might mention that section 7 deals with the enfranchisement of Indians.

I hope the minister is going to give the committee an explanation in connection with the payment of debts by Indians. A man came into my office last week who had sold a horse to an Indian for $150. He could not obtain payment and had obtained a judgment to get the horse back. He had had to pay his own costs and found he was unable to regain possession of the animal. He wanted to know if he had to lose everything or if the department would not interfere.

For the information of the hon. member I would direct his attention to section 105 of the act, which reads:
No person shall take any security or otherwise obtain any lien or charge, whether by mortgage, judgment or otherwise upon real or personal property of any Indian or non-treaty Indian, except on real or personal property subject to taxation under the last three preceding sections: Provided that any person selling any article to an Indian or non-treaty Indian may take security on such article for any part of the price thereof which is unpaid.
As I read the act, any person selling a binder, a horse, a pig or any chattel to an Indian has a right to take a lien upon that property in order to satisfy his just debt.
Does that mean that the lien must be registered with the department?
No.

I think it was last year I brought to the attention of the minister a question of the responsibility of the government in regard to Indians who own motor oars. This is a very serious matter. While they were driving along at a reckle'ss speed, they ran into this man's car. They were arrested, one being sent to gaol for sixty days and the other fined. At present in British Columbia an ordinary citizen, before he is permitted to drive a car, must have a driver's licence and also a licence for the car itself. But an Indian may purchase a car, either outright or on time, and he is let loose, so to speak, throughout the country. He know's he is a ward of the government. Under our laws it is true that the ordinary citizen may drive a car on the public streets without its being insured. If his car is in an accident he cannot run it again until he takes out insurance fully protecting the public. It is not so with the Indian. He may have as many accidents and cause as much injury a's he likes, and nothing can be done against him because he is a ward of the government, so long as the government does not allow the injured party to sue. As the Indian is the
Indian Act

ward of the government I believe the government should be responsible for the actions of its wards, just as a father is responsible for the actions of his minor children. Mr. MUPtPHY:	As the hon. member has
stated, he did draw this question to my attention some months ago, but I think he is in error when he states that an Indian can drive a motor car on the public highways without a licence. He may drive it on the reserve without a car licence or a driver's licence, but once he leaves the reserve, unless I am greatly mistaken, it is necessary for him to take out a car licence and a driver's licence.
The hon. member also raises the point of the Indian being an irresponsible party in case of a motor car accident, and he suggests that there should be some provision whereby the Indian would be held responsible. May I draw attention to the fact that there are many white people driving cars to-day who, if they are involved in an accident with their car, have no property which can be seized in case of a judgment against them not being settled. They are in just the same position as the Indian in that respect.
Not quite.
The white man has to have car insurance.

In some cases, but not in
all.
As a matter of fact, the Indian comes under the provincial law the moment he leaves the reserve.
The white man can only have an accident once without taking out insurance, but an Indian can have accidents repeatedly.

Not off the reserve, because the provincial authorities would have the right to refuse him a licence for his car and a driver's licence, and in that way the Indian could be made amenable to the provincial law. So I think the hon. member is wrong in his contention.

Might I explain that? The
white man is, like a dog, entitled to only one bite. In British Columbia, for instance, I 
think the white man is allowed to have only one accident before taking out insurance fully protecting the public. The people in British Columbia at any rate have recognized that they must protect the public against these accidents caused by irresponsible people. While the law as it stands is good so far as the white man is concerned, I think it should be amended to make it even more strict so that a man cannot cause an acident with his car once without the public being fully protected against damages. As it stands now, the white man must satisfy a judgment against him before he can run his car again. That is the inducement to take out insurance. More than that, he has not only to pay the judgment against him, but he cannot run his car again until he puts up a sum of money or takes out an insurance policy guaranteeing that he will be good for any future accidents in which his car may be involved. Where the law is lacking is that it should have in it this insurance principle to begin with. A man may be running a motor truck for his livelihood, and because he is involved in an accident he is deprived of his livelihood by a judgment, say, of five or six thousand dollars, which he will never be able to pay very probably, and he is thereby deprived of ever running a car again. Even where he is able to pay the judgment, he has to take out insurance.
While the minister is probably correct in saying that once the Indian leaves the reserve he comes under the provincial law as to driver's licence, car licence, and so forth, he is not responsible financially. In my own home town a white man was very badly injured in. a motor accident by an Indian, and under ordinary conditions he -would have got a judgment of perhaps two thousand dollars against a white man, but he did not get a cent because the man was an Indian. Now that Indian is not going to be warned by that accident, because he did not suffer in any way, and he can go out and do the same thing to-morrow. We want to see the Indian put on the same basis as the white man in regard to responsibility. In British Columbia at least, and I understand that Ontario is following very much along the same lines, we are guaranteeing the general public against serious material loss caused by irresponsible or careless drivers, but when it comes to the Indian we are absolutely hopeless and helpless.

With the general remarks of the hon. member I am rather in agreement, but I do not quite agree with him in his conclusion that there is nothing to prevent the Indian who has had one accident from

Indian Act
going out again and having another. The granting of the car licence and the driver's licence rests with the provincial government, and if the Indian is not considered by the provincial authorities a responsible party to put in control of a motor vehicle, all they have to do is to deprive him of his licence, and he is thereby deprived of the right to drive his car on the highways of the province.
I think, therefore, the hon. member is wrong in his contention.

But the civil law does not exist for the Indian, and that is the trouble. A man may cause serious damage with his car and yet not be deprived of his licence, and in the case of the Indian you have no recourse against him under the civil law. The civil law is taken away so far as the Indian is concerned.

I have not heard the whole discussion but I have not yet heard any explanation of the limitation in this section. Why is it confined to the reserves in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the territories? Why does not this provision apply to the other provinces in which there are reserves?
Mr. MlfRPHY: When this clause was first drafted, if my information is correct, it was drawn with particular reference to those provinces because it has been the policy of the department for a number of years to encourage the Indians in the western provinces named in this section to establish themselves by cultivating the land. It is there that the Indian who formerly obtained his livelihood through the chase, or by other means, has been induced to take up the arts of agriculture,, and in order to protect him during this process of transition from a nomadic state to that of a farmer it has been considered necessary to protect him in the disposal of his produce. That is the reason why these particular provinces are mentioned in the section.

The hon. minister and some hon. members have spoken of the irresponsibility of the Indian in the sale of his produce < and in regard to automobile accidents. I am afraid that this discussion will leave the public under a false impression that the Indians are responsible when they are outside the reserve. That is not the fact. But if I am wrong I should be very pleased if the minister would amend the legislation so that it would be absolutely indisputable that an Indian outside the reserve is responsible and that if he causes an accident or if he buys something he comes under the law just the same as the white man, who can be sued and judgment
obtained against him. If that is the fact, 1 should like to hear from the minister, and if not I beg, ask or pray that some amendments be made to the law for the protection of the public.

I believe the hon. member has read more into my remarks than I had intended to, or in fact did, convey. In no place in the Indian Act is the Indian described as a minor or a ward. I realize that those are terms generally used when speaking of Indians, but at no point in the act are they so described. Under the Indian Act he is described solely as an Indian. In some cases by treaty, and other cases by other means, he is given certain privileges, if they may be so called. Concerning the responsibilities of Indians on reserves, I should like to make some observations. If an Indian who has suit brought against him for damages has property off the reserve, he is in the same position as a w'hite man, but not in cases where his personal property is owned on the reserve.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	I have been a lawyer
for some time in the province of Quebec, and I believe the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville is labouring under a mistaken idea. The Indian is under the same responsibility as a white man; he has the same criminal responsibility; he cannot be granted a motor car licence unless that licence be issued by provincial authorities. He is subject to all the traffic regulations and motor laws of his province. If he causes damage, he is responsible. If he has property, his responsibility is the same as that of a white man who has property and causes damage. If he has no property we come to the old French dictum: La oil il n'y a rien le roi perd ses droits: "Where there is nothing the king loses his right." If the Indian owns the automobile, in the event of his causing damage, it can be seized.

No.
Mr. LaVERGNE :	The hon. member is
mistaken. In a case such as he has described the minor, or the Indian who is supposed to be a minor under the law, would be responsible. He is responsible for the damage he causes just the same as any other man would be. The father would be responsible only when he was aware of the minor's action, and when he had such action under his control and did not prevent it. Otherwise there could be no responsibility against a father. The minor must take the responsibility himself, and action could be taken only against him. It is the minor wdio pays and is respon-
Indian Act

sible for the damage he causes. In the same way a man who sells to an Indian knows very well what he is doing, and if he sells to one who has no goods or no property he must take the risk, in the same way as if he were selling to a white man, or to a minor who cannot contract. Nobody is supposed to ignore the law. But if an Indian has property, or if an object which he sells has a lien against it, under the law he is responsible. Therefore, unless my understanding is incorrect, I do not see how the cases outlined by the hon. members for Laprairie-Napier-ville and New Westminster can be dealt with by amendments to the Indian Act. Further than that, I believe no amendment to the Indian Act could interfere with the enforcement of provincial traffic or civil laws. Those remedies rest entirely within the control of the provinces. The only action we could take would be to change the statutes pertaining to Indians.

I think
Ontario law has gone that far.

Ontario law, but not Quebec law.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Yes, and Quebec law.
I have had some experience pleading for Indians.

If the hon. member for
Montmagny would permit me I should like to refer to a case in which the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville appeared. I refer to an action which arose from an automobile accident occuring outside a reserve. The client of the hon. member suffered personal injuries and also damage to his car. He tried to sue, but was informed that the Indian was a minor and was not responsible. I believe the department told him he had no recourse. The hon. member for Montmagny has said that the Indian is on the same footing as the white man; in my view he is mistaken. Particularly is that so in the province of Quebec, and I believe his interpretation of the law would be as incorrect in regard to the other Canadian provinces. The stand taken by the Department of Indian Affairs is to the effect that Indians are not responsible. They hold that if an Indian, the owner of property, goes outside a reserve with an automobile and causes damage, but returns to the reserve, he is above the law, and nobody can sue him. To be more accurate, he could be sued, but there could be no execution against him.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	I believe the hon.
member is wrong in that.

Seizure of the car could be made only when it is outside the reserve. I believe if the hon. member would inquire from the minister he would learn that my information is correct.
Mr. LaVERGNE: I am not quite certain, but I believe that under the act any bailiff can enter a reserve and seize the personal goods of an Indian.

No.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	That is a matter however which is subject to discussion, and I must say I have heard arguments and have had judgments both ways. I am inclined to believe that if the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville had gone to the court and not to the department he would have got redress.

I have obtained judgment
in court, but could not get execution.
Mr. LaVERGNE : I do not know whether I should blame the Indian, the judge or the lawyer; I am sure however it was not the lawyer. As the hon. member knows, there are some bad judgments handed out. The responsibility of the Indian exists absolutely within the law; he is responsible [DOT]ivilly and criminally. So far as civil responsibility is concerned there is no difference between a white man and an Indian. The point is to know how much of the damage can be repaired. In that case again the Indian is in the same position as the white man who has no money or property, or whose automobile is not paid for. I must close my remarks, because I must not set a bad example by being out of order myself.

The hon. member's remarks are most interesting.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	I believe the Indian
should be enfranchised, and so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, with special reference to Two Mountains, St. Regis and Caughnawaga; I believe they could claim franchise. They are here under special treaty with the King of France. At the time of the conquest they became subject to govern- , mental authority, just the same as the other inhabitants of the country. They are British citizens, just the same as we Canadians of French origin. I understand, however, that many of the Indian bands in the province of Quebec do not want the ballot; they prefer to be wards of the nation. They have certain privileges which they do not want to give up for the fallacy, shall I call it, of the ballot. Of course usually the ballot does good, but sometimes it goes astray. I do

Indian Act
not think we can do anything here to meet the complaints brought up by the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville and the hon. member for New Westminster. These matters rest entirely with the provinces. If an amendment were passed here certainly it would be ultra vires; it would be encroaching on the rights of the provinces.

I do not wish to delay the committee, but I should like to ask one question which might clear up a lot of doubt. My information is that an Indian, though he may own property on the reserve, cannot be sued for damages outside the reserve. That is my information, and that always has been my opinion. The Indian can be prosecuted and put in jail, but I understand that he cannot be sued for damages. I should like to ask the minister whether or not that is correct.

Not being a member of the legal fraternity or a judge I do not know that I am in a position to give a categorical answer to that question. However, my information would lead me to the conclusion that an Indian may be sued, though I am not altogether certain that if a judgment were obtained in favour of the plaintiff it could be ent'oroed. My information is to the effect that if an Indian owns property outside the boundaries of a reserve he is in the same position as a white man. Property within the reserve would be exempt from the enforcement of such a judgment, but if in the opinion of the court such property did not belong to the reserve-a motor car, for instance-it might be seized in execution of the judgment.

Section agreed to.
Section 4 agreed to.
On section 5-Roads.
I should like to ask the minister if this gives the Superintendent General authority to over-ride the Indian council.
Yes, I think it does.

I have not the act before me, but I thought that in all cases the Superintendent General had power to over-ride the actions of the Indian councils. I just wondered why you should ask for this particular power.
At present there is nothing in the act which gives the minister any such specific authority, and that is why we are asking for it now.

I was referring to the general authority possessed by the Superintendent General to control the Indians and their councils if the occasion should arise. The only reason I asked the question was because I wondered why this particular case should be specified.
It was to enable the Superintendent Getneml to deal with any particular case that might come up in connection with the location of a road.

I agree with the principle, but here is the point: I under stood that the over-riding clause was general in its application to the whole act; it is an arbitrary right, but I believe it is necessary. My fear is that you will be asked to specify all cases in which this right exists. If you simply take one case and say it is necessary for the Superintendent General to have the authority to over-ride the council with respect to any road or road allowance I am afraid you are weakening his authority generally under the act.

I am just a little curious about this section. Why should the Superintendent General have the right to say where a road should go within a reserve, when he probably never sees the reserve and knows nothing about it.

Of course the Superintendent General would act upon the advice of the surveyor who determined in the first place the proper location for the road. Certainly the minister would avail himself of all possible information before making a decision.

I am interested in the application of this section, and I should like to preface the question I am about to ask by stating an actual case. In my constituency there are seven reserves, four of which come under what is known as the Crooked Lake agency. Crooked Lake is in a widening of the Qu'Appelle valley; it is about a mile and a half wide and about fifteen miles long. On one side of this lake there is a splendid beach, and many people living in the southeastern part of the province have established cottages at this point. In order to get to their camps they have to cross a portion of the reserve at the west end of the lake. From time to time they have had considerable difficulty with the Indians on the reserve, since they are really trespassers when they cross. Two years ago we presented a petition to the department in an effort to get a road put through the reserve, but on that occasion the Indians refused to consent to the

Indian Act

proposition. I should like to ask the minister whether, under this section, it would be possible to take any action in this respect. There are about thirty camps in this vicinty, and I should like to know whether it would be possible for the government to open a road through the reserve which would give these people access to the beach.

This amendment was not designed for the purpose of giving the Superintendent General authority, generally speaking, to override the desires of the Indians. It was rather designed for a purpose such as this; suppose it is in the interests of the Indians to locate the road through that reserve. We send a surveyor from the department for the purpose of locating that road, which they themselves are willing to have constructed. The surveyor makes a report to the department as to the proper location of that road. But for some reason a few Indians may object to that location. Their reasons may or may not be well founded. In those cases it is considered by the department that the authority should rest with the Superintendent General, after receiving the best advice he can get, to determine the location of that road.
Before giving a specific answer to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle I would say that any minister charged with the responsibility of conducting Indian affairs would have to give very serious consideration to the question whether he should, in direct opposition to the general wishes of the Indians, place a road through the reserve for the sole benefit, shall we say, of white people. It was not the intention in drafting this amendment to give to the superintendent that power, or to exercise that power in that particular way, but rather to exercise it in the way I have indicated.

I quite
agree with everything the minister has said on the case cited by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle. If agreement could not be secured from the Indians the Superintendent General has authority to do these things. He may not exercise that authority, but it is given him by the act. My only reason for asking about the insertion of this particular clause was to learn why it was taken out of the general provisions of authority and segregated as dealing with roads only. I can oite a number of cases in which this particular question has arisen before. We have had difficulties with the Indian council, who are not in agreement with the provincial authorities usually when these projected highways have to pass through their reserve.

If my hon. friend will
permit me, this is really to deal with roads in reserves for the benefit of the Indians, but not having reference to provincial highways, in respect of which expropriation powers can be exercised.

I thought
the Superintendent General had this power. I have not the act before me, but he has very wide powers. My curiosity was aroused to know just why they are asking for this specific power.
Progress reported.

speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL-ALLEGED MALADMINISTRATION IN MARINE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish, before going into supply, to bring to the notice of the house a question of maladministration in a department. I am sorry to see that the minister in charge is not in the house, the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau).
In these days when the government is at its wits' end for money, when cuts have to be made in almost eveiy estimate, and when economy has to be practised to the extent that it almost becomes false economy, it very much becomes the government and the several departments to be particularly careful to prevent anything that savours of waste, uselessness, abuse or graft, to avoid what is called even the appearance of evil. The policy I have adopted in such matters if such have been brought to my attention has been this; I would bring the matter complained of to the attention of the particular minister, and if he took steps to rectify it, to get restitution from the parties concerned if it were a case of money improperly spent, and to check the abuse complained of, I was satisfied with that and the matter went no further. I did not bring it to the floor of the house or the public platform and seek to make political capital of it. Some of the minister's colleagues are aware that I have acted in that way. But, in a case where they refuse to take any action, propose to brazen it out as justified, then I think it is my duty to bring the matter to the attention of the house, not only as a

Marine-Alleged Maladministration
warning to others but to demonstrate to my constituents that I at least have no part or parcel in the transaction complained of.
Through nearly all these matters of complaint, in my district at any rate, I find running the black thread of the abuse of government patronage; government patronage somewhat crudely manipulated through the agency of a gentleman who is euphemistically described as the government representative in the district of Comox-Albemi, in sharp contrast to the representative of the people, the man they elected to represent them in parliament. This system, or lack of system, is of course entirely subversive of the democratic form of government under which we are supposed to live. It leads to autocratic and almost despotic use of power for which there is no authority granted by any section of the people. We were told in bygone centuries that kings governed by divine right. But this is beyond that, they do not even pretend to have divine right, they derive this power, which is too often a temptation to abuse, from the mere fact that they are associated with some political party.
The instance to which I wish to draw attention centres around a man whom I am not going to name because I do not wish to hold him up to public obloquy too much. I will merely describe him as Mr. Man. He possesses a somewhat peculiar entity. A couple of generations ago theological circles were much exercised by consideration of the true meaning to be ascribed to the idea of the Trinity. Did it really mean what it said or was it a figure of speech, the idea of three in one and one in three, yet not three, but one and yet not one, but three? I am confronted with the extension of this puzzling doctrine to this gentleman because of the combination of identities. It is not only a case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, it is a sort of square-root problem because he possesses not one entity but four, yet he is not four men but only one.
The first official appearance, and in which he does not appear as a returned man, is that of mail carrier. This position was formerly held by a married man and was given to this man without advertising or without recourse to the Civil Service Commission. He draws only the sum of 810 per month, not a large amount but nevertheless there are thousands of single men to-day in British Columbia and probably in other parts of Canada upon relief who receive only S6 per month. I am sure that a man receiving S10 per month would have to have very strong political pull in order to obtain any relief.
53719-132%
One would think that this might suffice, but there is a second reincarnation in which he appears, and again not as a returned man- that of provincial road foreman on relief work. This is a sort of intermittent position, it runs on a sliding scale. If any other of his positions come into the landscape and he is afforded an opportunity of earning some money, the relief work is shut down and the mien sent home until he has completed the work upon his other position or positions, when he has nothing else to do he returns to the relief work.
His third identity, again not as a returned man, is as a patrolman. For some years he has he'd this position which operates for four months in the year and pays, I believe, $90 per month. I understand there is a section in the Civil Service Act which states that a man shall not hold two positions. I do not think it says a man shall not hold four positions, but apparently it was not contemplated that such a thing would happen. It might be thought that a man working four months in the year and receiving $90 per month might well be able to make way for someone harder up than himself. I think I can say without fear of contradiction that anyone in British Columbia would have to possess very strong political pull to be able to get any relief while holding a position bringing in S350 a year. I said he was not a returned man, but he displaced a returned man. This man had a particularly fine record both as a soldier and as a patrolman, so much so that the permanent officials complimented him upon his work. My statement can be checked up when I say that there was not the least tinge of suspicion of any political action on the part of this man which would justify his being let out or not being reappointed.
So there are three positions which we find Mr. Man occupying. One would think that that would suffice, but we find him, again not as a returned man, in another reincarnation, as contractor to the government of the day. Before I give the particulars of this position perhaps I should refer to another situation which may explain the other four. This man was prominent in politics and during one of his periods of employment as patrolman he took four days off in order to attend a political convention-the government paid him for those four days. Perhaps this political association explains in part the other four activities which providence has been so kind as to bestow upon him. Contractors have beer; known to lose money even when dealing with, a government but I do not think anyone

Marine-Alleged Maladministration
would be so foolish or so ill-advised as to lose money when allowed to write his own ticket. This man was allowed to write his own contract which stated very definitely the money he was to receive and very indefinitely the work he was to perform in order to receive that money. The work he was to do consisted of repairing some five bridges on a trail, each one four to six feet wide. The usual method adopted in such a case by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) would be to have an engineer report upon the necessities and requirements of the work. The marine department has an engineer directly in charge of this work and located not very far away. One would suppose that specifications would be prepared by an engineer and tenders invited and that, all things being equal, the lowest tender would be accepted possibly with the requirement that a bond be furnished that the work would be carried out.

Is the hon. gentleman
speaking of dominion work?

Yes, these bridges are on a
life-saving trail managed by the Department of Marine and under direct charge of its engineer.

speechtext: On the trail between Bamfield and Pachena. One would have expected that all these reasonable and sensible regulations would have been carried out in disposing of this matter, but in fact none of them were-I am told that an estimate of a sort was made by a certain gentleman I have the very highest regard for this man in his own particular line of business, he is a man of outstanding ability in that regard but he is not an engineer; he is not qualified to do work of this kind, more especially when there is an engineer in charge of the work.
